common_name: Shinko Asian Pear (Fire Blight-Resistant Russet Japanese Pear)

planting.note: Plant bare-root while dormant in late winter; needs roughly 400-450 chill hours and a different Asian pear cultivar such as Hosui or Twentieth Century nearby for pollination.

directions: Set the bare-root tree in well-drained soil with the graft union above grade, then train to an open-center or central-leader form and thin developing fruit to one per cluster for larger size. Shinko is prized among Asian pear growers for its unusually strong resistance to fire blight, a major limitation for pear culture in humid climates, while still producing sweet, mildly tangy, crisp bronze-russeted fruit. Harvest in late summer to early fall once the fruit slips easily from the spur, and expect a productive, long-lived tree once established.

common_name: Limbertwig Apple (Old Fashioned Southern Appalachian Heirloom)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant; this Appalachian heirloom wants roughly 700-800 chill hours, so it performs best in the mountain and upper piedmont South rather than the Gulf Coast.

directions: Stake young trees loosely, since the cultivar takes its name from the distinctively supple, drooping branches that bend rather than break under a heavy crop. Limbertwig is really an old Southern Appalachian family name covering many closely related strains, so trees sold under this name can vary somewhat, but all share a rich, spicy-tart flavor that many growers feel improves after a few weeks in storage. It was a dooryard and cider staple across the Southern mountains through the 19th century and is still sought out by heirloom orchardists for its complex, old-fashioned flavor and long keeping quality.
sources: Creighton Lee Calhoun, Old Southern Apples

common_name: Mammoth Black Twig Apple (Paragon, Arkansas Black Twig)

planting.note: Plant bare-root while dormant in a sunny, well-drained site; needs about 700-800 chill hours and benefits from a nearby pollinator such as Winesap or Grimes Golden.

directions: Give this vigorous tree plenty of room and prune annually to keep the spreading, upright canopy open to light and air. Originating in Arkansas in the 1830s as a Winesap seedling, Mammoth Black Twig became a popular commercial apple across the South and lower Midwest for its large size, dark red color, and firm, tart-sweet flesh that stores well into winter. It is a distinct cultivar from the unrelated Arkansas Black and is grown today mainly by heirloom orchardists and collectors seeking a taste of 19th-century Southern apple culture.

planting.note: Plant bare-root in late winter; a moderate chill requirement of roughly 500-600 hours makes it more heat-adapted than most heirloom apples and a good fit for the middle and lower South.

directions: Plant in full sun with good air movement, since this large, vigorous tree was historically valued for its toughness and reliability rather than fussy care. Nickajack was one of the most widely planted apples in the antebellum and postbellum South, grown from the Appalachians to Texas for its large greenish-red fruit, dependable annual crops, and good keeping quality in a root cellar. Flavor is mildly subacid rather than showy, making it best suited to cooking, drying, and cider as well as fresh eating once fully ripe.

common_name: Kinnard's Choice Apple (Tennessee Heirloom Dessert Apple)

planting.note: Plant bare-root while dormant; needs roughly 600-700 chill hours, well suited to the upper and middle South.

directions: Grow as a standard tree in deep, well-drained soil and thin fruit clusters to improve size and reduce limb breakage in heavy years. Kinnard's Choice originated in Tennessee in the 19th century and has long been prized by Southern heirloom apple collectors for its rich, aromatic, exceptionally sweet flesh, considered by many old-timers to be among the best-flavored dessert apples of the region. It ripens in late summer to early fall and is primarily grown today by small orchardists and heritage-fruit enthusiasts rather than commercial producers.

common_name: Virginia Beauty Apple (Spicy Russeted Virginia Heirloom)

planting.note: Plant bare-root while dormant in a sunny, well-drained site; requires roughly 700 chill hours, so it is best suited to the upper and middle South rather than low-chill Gulf Coast areas.

directions: Plant in a sheltered but sunny site and prune to an open canopy to help the fruit color and to control the tree's tendency toward biennial bearing. Virginia Beauty is a late-19th-century Virginia heirloom noted for its striped red skin, patches of russet, and distinctively spicy, aromatic flesh that improves in flavor during a few weeks of storage. It has long been a favorite among Southern heritage orchardists for fresh eating and cider, prized as much for its complex flavor as for its keeping ability into winter.

common_name: Ben Davis Apple (Mortgage Lifter Apple, New York Pippin)

planting.note: Plant bare-root while dormant; moderate chill requirement of about 600-700 hours and notable tolerance of heat, drought, and poor soils made it a favorite pioneer-era orchard apple across a wide range of climates.

directions: Ben Davis tolerates less-than-ideal soil and irregular watering better than most apples, making it forgiving for beginning orchardists or marginal sites. Introduced in the early 1800s and possibly of Kentucky or Tennessee origin, it became one of the most widely planted commercial apples in 19th-century America, prized for its precocious, heavy, reliable annual crops and its exceptional storage life rather than for outstanding fresh flavor, which is mild and somewhat bland compared to dessert apples. It remains of interest to homesteaders and heirloom growers today mainly for its toughness, productivity, and long keeping quality in cold storage.

common_name: Old Home Pear (Fire Blight-Resistant European Pear)

planting.note: Plant bare-root in fall or late winter; needs roughly 600-700 chill hours and is especially valuable where humid summers bring heavy fire blight pressure.

directions: Plant in full sun with good air circulation, and prune lightly since vigorous new growth is the most blight-susceptible tissue on a pear tree. Old Home was released by USDA breeders in Oregon in the early 20th century and is famous chiefly for its outstanding resistance to fire blight, the disease that devastates most European pears in the humid Southeast, and it is widely used as a parent of blight-resistant rootstocks as well as a scion cultivar in its own right. The medium-sized, yellow-green fruit is firm and good for canning and baking, and a second pear cultivar such as Bartlett or Moonglow should be planted nearby for reliable pollination.
